::: {.lead}
Sexual violence is measured through people's reported experiences, police records and the response of public services. Each reveals part of the picture. Comparing countries starts with identifying which part each number describes.

Sources: [WHO data portal][who-data], [ONS latest crime bulletin][ons-2026], [ONS childhood bulletin][ons-child]. These are different populations and periods, not three comparable rates.

## What the evidence shows

**The international comparison is narrower than “all sexual assault”.** WHO's harmonised non-partner measure estimates UK lifetime prevalence at **7.3%**, with a **95% uncertainty interval of 4.6%–11.0%**, among women aged 15 and over. It excludes violence by a current or former intimate partner. The portal labels the territory United Kingdom; this should not be confused with the England and Wales crime survey. [Explore the worldwide comparison](worldwide.qmd).

**The latest England and Wales adult survey starts a new series.** The redesigned sexual-victimisation questions produce an estimate of around **one million people** affected in the last year. The measure includes experiences beyond contact assault and cannot be joined to the former sexual-assault trend. [Read the UK detail](uk.qmd).

**Childhood experiences need their own account.** UNICEF's estimates concern experiences before age 18 among people alive at estimation. ONS asks adults to recall their childhood. Neither is an annual estimate of abuse among today's children. [Read the childhood chapter](children.qmd).

**Recorded offences and justice outcomes reveal institutional demand and response.** They cannot establish how common sexual violence is in the whole population. A charge is not a conviction, and an early charge rate changes as investigations conclude. [Read the justice chapter](justice.qmd).

::: {.reading-note}
**How to read “UK”.** England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have separate statistical systems and legal contexts. This report names the jurisdiction on every UK figure. It does not relabel England and Wales as the whole United Kingdom.
:::

## Start with the question

| Your question | Evidence to use | What it cannot establish |
|---|---|---|
| How many people report an experience? | Population surveys; harmonised WHO estimates | Every unreported or undisclosed experience |
| What has reached the police? | Recorded offences and their source definitions | A ranking of countries by actual victimisation |
| What happened to recorded investigations? | Home Office outcome cohorts | The probability that every assault leads to conviction |
| What happened during childhood? | Retrospective surveys; UNICEF estimates | Current annual child prevalence |
